Title: Senate Panel Passes Bill to Reverse Dismantling of Education Department

URL Source: https://www.the74million.org/article/senate-panel-passes-bill-to-reverse-dismantling-of-education-department

Published Time: 2026-07-30T16:15:35-04:00

Markdown Content:
_Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox._[**Sign up for The 74 Newsletter**](https://www.the74million.org/about/newsletters/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=top&utm_id=newsletter)

_Updated_

A Senate committee advanced legislation Thursday aimed at undoing the Trump administration’s efforts to split apart the U.S. Department of Education. The bill delivers the plan the biggest rebuke since Education Secretary Linda McMahon began shifting offices to other agencies last year.

The education committee’s [bill](https://www.help.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/64d0ff0c-bc73-9a98-3c30-c7a5297a33d6/S.%205046%20SxS_004e71c7-1876-475b-8c65-eb3ffbbc84b9.pdf) would keep oversight of K-12 and services for students with disabilities at the department. It would also keep the Office of Postsecondary Education out of the Department of Labor and the Office of Indian Education from moving to the Department of the Interior.

The legislation leaves “landmark education programs,” like Title I and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act “at the Department of Education where Congress specifically put them and where they belong,” said Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, who along with GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, co-sponsored the bill with Sen. Tim Kaine, a Virginia Democrat.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, the Louisiana Republican who chairs the committee, voted no on the bill, saying that he’s open to moving some programs, but opposes giving the Department of Health and Human Services responsibility for special education. That move treats “students with disabilities as patients to diagnose rather than learners to educate,” he said, adding that he doubts that any Education Department staff transferred there would be “empowered and prioritized” to do their jobs.

Despite the bipartisan support for leaving much of the department intact, nine members, all Republicans, voted against it. “Many of us have long believed that the federal footprint in education is much larger than it needs to be,” said Republican Sen. Tommy Tuberville of Alabama.

Following the vote, McMahon and six other Trump cabinet members [sent Congress a letter](https://www.ed.gov/media/document/secretary-mcmahon-and-partner-agencies-letter-congressional-leadership-114341.pdf) saying there are “misconceptions” about the agreements and they just need more time to prove they’ll work. They have already “demonstrated measurable results by driving stronger grant competitions, streamlining government operations and producing better outcomes for Americans,” they wrote.

Political observers have said since the beginning that the administration’s plan to eliminate the department doesn’t stand a chance of passing the Senate, and Thursday was evidence of that. The legislation, however, still needs to pass the full Senate and is a sharp contrast to the package of 10 bills the House education committee moved earlier this month formalizing the movement of most key programs out of the department. While House Republicans call the arrangements “reform,” the actions have prompted Rep. Suzanne Bonamici to launch an impeachment effort against McMahon. The Oregon Democrat says the agreements are illegal and that the Republicans’ bills are an attempt “to cover for the unlawful actions already taken.”

Even if the House passes those 10 bills, it’s highly unlikely they would ever get votes in the Senate, said David Cleary, a principal with The Group, a Washington lobbying firm and a former Republican education staffer for the Senate.

The Senate bill, he added, might not go any further either. It’s possible, he said, that Collins and Murkowski could attach it as an amendment to the [budget resolution](https://budget.house.gov/press-release/house-advances-reconciliation-to-support-our-troops-and-secure-our-elections) for defense spending that Republicans are trying to pass through a process known as reconciliation. But even then, it might fail, Cleary said.

During that July 15 markup in the House, Democratic Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia said that the proposals don’t do anything to fulfill McMahon’s promise to “return education to the states.”

“You’re just moving people around Washington D.C.,” he said.

On Thursday, Democratic Sen. Patty Murray of Washington pressed the department to disclose how much the moves are costing taxpayers.

The Senate bill includes her amendment requiring McMahon to provide Congress with quarterly reports on how much the department is spending to implement the agreements. The department, so far, has spent $1 million to move just one relatively small office running [career and technical education](https://www.acteonline.org/blog/cte-policy-watch/house-holds-full-committee-markup-on-bills-to-make-interagency-agreements-permanent/)to the Department of Labor, and the administration is asking for an [additional $9 million](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/general/budget/2027/CBJ-2027-V1-08.pdf) to hire more staff to help with the transition.

“If you’re proud of this deal, show us the price tag,” Murray said. “What do you have to hide?”

Murray also offered separate amendments to reverse all of the agreements, including relocating the Office for Civil Rights to the Department of Justice, but those didn’t pass the committee. Collins said she’s in favor of letting the Justice Department take over education civil rights investigations because she said OCR has failed to address anti-semitism on college campuses.

But Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, a Democrat, said the move won’t improve conditions for Jewish students because the administration has downsized the civil rights workforce.

“We are at a 12-year low in terms of the number of cases that are being resolved,” he said. DOJ is “just out of the business of trying to investigate serious instances of civil rights abuse.”

Of all the interagency agreements, placing special education within HHS has received the most attention. One advocacy group supports the change, arguing that the shift would offer families more resources when their children transition out of the K-12 system. Out of the [Administration for Community Living](https://acl.gov/about-community-living), HHS already runs federally funded programs for adults with disabilities.

“Too many students leave school without a clear path to a meaningful career, education or training path,” Rachel Barkley, director of Able Americans, wrote in [a recent commentary](https://ableamericans.us/rachel-barkley-moving-special-ed-programs-to-hhs-removes-siloes-in-the-disability-system/).

But overall, [the actions](https://www.ed.gov/media/document/ed-and-hhs-interagency-osers-partnership-updated-61526-114241.pdf) have been highly unpo

articles.full_body:
Title: Senate Panel Advances Science of Reading, Dyslexia Bills with Bipartisan Support

URL Source: https://www.the74million.org/article/senate-panel-advances-science-of-reading-dyslexia-bills-with-bipartisan-support

Published Time: 2026-07-30T14:42:32-04:00

Markdown Content:
_Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox._[**Sign up for The 74 Newsletter**](https://www.the74million.org/about/newsletters/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=top&utm_id=newsletter)

A bill that would require states to only use the science of reading in classrooms in order to qualify for a multi-million dollar funding grant passed with bipartisan support from a committee of federal lawmakers Thursday morning.

The [READ Act](https://www.help.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/64d0ff0c-bc73-9a98-3c30-c7a5297a33d6/S.%204689_b59cfe54-a5cf-4f63-8337-e377cbfdb466.pdf) (S.4689) would strengthen the federal government’s oversight of the science of reading through amendments to the [Comprehensive Literacy State Development grant](http://www.ed.gov/grants-and-programs/grants-birth-grade-12/well-rounded-education-grants/comprehensive-literacy-state-development), which currently provides $194 million to aid literacy instruction in 23 states.

“Capable students are dropping out of high school simply because they were never taught to read,” said U.S. Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee chairman Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana. “This legislation aims to address the national literacy crisis by strengthening evidence-based literacy instruction … and empowering states, local communities and parents with more resources.”

After the bill’s 20-2 passage out of the Senate HELP Committee, it now heads to the floor for a full senate vote. Other bills, including one that would explicitly identify dyslexia as a learning disability under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, also passed Thursday.

The READ Act closely mirrors and expands on [a similar bill that unanimously passed](https://www.the74million.org/article/bipartisan-science-of-reading-bill-passes-house-committee/) the House of Representative’s Education Committee in March, but has not yet been taken up for a full House vote.

Both the Senate and House bill aim to define the science of reading in federal law as instruction that teaches phonics and phonemic awareness and also builds vocabulary, fluency, comprehension, oral language and writing skills.

A [report released earlier this year](https://www.the74million.org/article/report-nearly-one-third-of-teachers-still-use-discredited-reading-methods/) found nearly a third of teachers still used “discredited” methods to teach kids how to read and aren’t fully committed to the science of reading. Both bills, however, would reject the use of federal funds for other teaching methods, such as three-cueing, where students are asked to figure out unfamiliar words through context clues or pictures.

The READ Act further includes proposals for prioritizing federal support for the bottom 10% of underperforming states and shifting funding of individual literacy projects to more systematic widespread efforts like requirements for early literacy screening.

It also has language that calls for teacher preparation program audits, expands professional development opportunities and creates new requirements for states to provide more detailed annual reports with the number of students receiving intervention, the number of teachers receiving professional development and the number of districts using high-quality learning materials aligned with the science of reading if they’re receiving the grant.

Keri Rodrigues, co-founder and president of the National Parents Union, said the bill’s passage out of committee is the result of years of advocacy from families.

“This is a bill that codifies the fact that the sky is blue,” Rodrigues said. “We’re just very excited that folks are seeing the importance of this, and we’re able to finally get [lawmakers] to show they can prioritize kids, they can be swayed based on evidence, they can actually make good decisions for kids and frankly do the right thing in what is a very difficult political climate.”

Lawmakers on Thursday also considered the [21st Century Dyslexia Act](https://www.help.senate.gov/hearings/the-following-agenda-to-be-considered-07-29-2026) (S.3010), another piece of legislation that would affect students who are learning to read.

The 21st Century Dyslexia Act proposed to add and explicitly define dyslexia as a disability covered under the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act — requiring schools to provide accommodations and other services needed for dyslexic students to be successful in the classroom.

Under IDEA, students with “[specific learning disabilities](https://sites.ed.gov/idea/regs/b/a/300.8/c/10)” are protected, but Cassidy argued that making dyslexia a disability category — similar to what was done with [autism in 1990](https://educationonline.ku.edu/community/idea-timeline) — would “increase screening, identification and the number of students receiving appropriate accommodations.”

“When reading scores haven’t moved and 20% of readers are dyslexic — and therefore learn to read differently — we either choose or choose not to do something positive for these students,” Cassidy said. “If we’re serious about addressing the inexcusably low literacy rates, we must pass this bill.”

More than a dozen organizations, including The Reading League, National Center for Learning Disabilities and International Dyslexia Association [opposed the legislation](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1PohHR9Jhiko9tGdt4vfv6GjIfc5kkTaF/edit), with concerns it would undermine support and confuse states.

In a written statement, the organizations also argued the legislation could be harmful because it used an outdated definition of dyslexia from the early 2000s. A new definition, which removed old IQ-discrepancy requirements, was [published last year](https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/what-a-new-dyslexia-definition-could-mean-for-schools/2025/11) from the International Dyslexia Association.

Democratic lawmakers, such as Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, brought up the challenges Thursday.

“There are 27 states, including Indiana, Florida, Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina, that effectively ban the use of this definition. Congress banned the use of this definition in the 2004 version of the IDEA,” Murphy said. “When you define dyslexia as relational between intelligence and reading ability, … many students with dyslexia … are judged to have lower intelligence levels. They don’t get services because you essentially have to show that there is a substantial difference between your reading ability and your assessed level of intelligence.”

The education committee’s [bill](https://www.help.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/64d0ff0c-bc73-9a98-3c30-c7a5297a33d6/S.%205046%20SxS_004e71c7-1876-475b-8c65-eb3ffbbc84b9.pdf) would keep oversight of K-12 and services for students with disabilities at the department. It would also keep the Office of Postsecondary Education out of the Department of Labor and the Office of Indian Education from moving to the Department of the Interior.

The legislation leaves “landmark education programs,” like Title I and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act “at the Department of Education where Congress specifically put them and where they belong,” said Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, who along with GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, co-sponsored the bill with Sen. Tim Kaine, a Virginia Democrat.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, the Louisiana Republican who chairs the committee, voted no on the bill, saying that he’s open to moving some programs, but opposes giving the Department of Health and Human Services responsibility for special education. That move treats “students with disabilities as patients to diagnose rather than learners to educate,” he said, adding that he doubts that any Education Department staff transferred there would be “empowered and prioritized” to do their jobs.

Despite the bipartisan support for leaving much of the department intact, nine members, all Republicans, voted against it. “Many of us have long believed that the federal footprint in education is much larger than it needs to be,” said Republican Sen. Tommy Tuberville of Alabama.

Following the vote, McMahon and six other Trump cabinet members [sent Congress a letter](https://www.ed.gov/media/document/secretary-mcmahon-and-partner-agencies-letter-congressional-leadership-114341.pdf) saying there are “misconceptions” about the agreements and they just need more time to prove they’ll work. They have already “demonstrated measurable results by driving stronger grant competitions, streamlining government operations and producing better outcomes for Americans,” they wrote.

fact_packs.headline: Senate Panel Advances Science of Reading, Dyslexia Bills with Bipartisan Support
facts: Title: Senate Panel Advances Science of Reading, Dyslexia Bills with Bipartisan Support

_Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox._[**Sign up for The 74 Newsletter**](https://www.the74million.org/about/newsletters/?utm_source=website&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=top&utm_id=newsletter)

A bill that would require states to only use the science of reading in classrooms in order to qualify for a multi-million dollar funding grant passed with bipartisan support from a committee of federal lawmakers Thursday morning.

The [READ Act](https://www.help.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/64d0ff0c-bc73-9a98-3c30-c7a5297a33d6/S.%204689_b59cfe54-a5cf-4f63-8337-e377cbfdb466.pdf) (S.4689) would strengthen the federal government’s oversight of the science of reading through amendments to the [Comprehensive Literacy State Development grant](http://www.ed.gov/grants-and-programs/grants-birth-grade-12/well-rounded-education-grants/comprehensive-literacy-state-development), which currently provides $194 million to aid literacy instr

“Capable students are dropping out of high school simply because they were never taught to read,” said U.S. Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee chairman Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana. “This legislation aims to address the national literacy crisis by strengthening evidence-based literacy instruction … and empowering states, local communities and parents with more resources.”

After the bill’s 20-2 passage out of the Senate HELP Committee, it now heads to the floor for a full senate vote. Other bills, including one that would explicitly identify dyslexia as a learning disability under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, also passed Thursday.

The READ Act closely mirrors and expands on [a similar bill that unanimously passed](https://www.the74million.org/article/bipartisan-science-of-reading-bill-passes-house-committee/) the House of Representative’s Education Committee in March, but has not yet been taken up for a full House vote.

Both the Senate and House bill aim to define the science of reading in federal law as instruction that teaches phonics and phonemic awareness and also builds vocabulary, fluency, comprehension, oral language and writing skills.
